name: Essential oil mouthwash (Listerine)

lead: Essential oil mouthwash, best known as Listerine, combines thymol, menthol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate. People use it daily for fresher breath and cleaner teeth and gums. It has been sold since 1879 and was the first US over-the-counter mouthwash.

The oils are described as disrupting bacterial cell walls, inhibiting enzymes and penetrating plaque biofilm. Systematic reviews find it reduces plaque and gingivitis versus brushing alone, and a commentary on a 2011 review found it may match chlorhexidine for long-term gum control while chlorhexidine is stronger on plaque.

paras: It is a standard daily rinse after brushing and flossing, used in many breath and gum care routines. Original and alcohol-free versions are both sold.
Original versions contain roughly 22 to 27 percent ethanol, which can cause burning or dryness; alcohol-free versions exist. Wikipedia describes the alcohol and oral cancer link as inconclusive.

angle.text: Listerine-style rinses are used daily for fresher breath and cleaner teeth and gums, with antiseptic oils cutting plaque and gingivitis. Trials show a modest reduction, with chlorhexidine still stronger on plaque.

lead: Essential oil mouthwash is a rinse whose active ingredients are thymol, menthol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate, best known as Listerine. Listerine was developed in 1879 by St. Louis chemist Joseph Lawrence and named after surgeon Joseph Lister.[1]

A 2011 systematic review compared essential oil rinses with chlorhexidine for plaque and gingival inflammation, and a commentary on it concluded the oil rinses may be equivalent for long-term gingival control while chlorhexidine performs better on plaque.[2][3] Essential oil rinses are used in many looksmaxxing oral care routines for breath and gum care.

paras: Lawrence licensed the formula to Jordan Wheat Lambert in 1881; it was promoted to dentists in 1895 and became the first over-the-counter mouthwash in the US in 1914.[1] In the 1920s Gerard Lambert marketed it against chronic halitosis, and from 1921 to the mid-1970s it was also sold for colds and sore throats, claims the FTC ruled misleading in 1976.[1] Pfizer acquired Warner-Lambert in 2000 and Johnson and Johnson bought Pfizer consumer healthcare in 2006.[1]

The original formula contains eucalyptol, thymol, methyl salicylate and menthol in an ethanol base of about 21.6 to 26.9 percent.[1] A review states the essential oils kill microorganisms by disrupting cell walls and inhibiting enzymes, and discusses penetration of plaque biofilm.[4] A 2015 laboratory study tested individual Listerine components and mixtures against oral bacteria.[5]

Wikipedia cites reductions of 22.2 percent in plaque and 28.2 percent in gingivitis after six months, only slightly above the vehicle without essential oils (20.8 and 27.7 percent).[1] A 3-day plaque model compared essential oil rinses with and without alcohol, and a feasibility study tested an alcohol-free essential oil rinse in institutionalised elders.[6][7] A trial in intensive care patients tested an essential oil rinse for mouth malodour.[8] A 1990 paper compared mechanical devices with antimicrobial rinses.[9]

Human studies include plaque models, trials in ICU patients and elders, and a radiotherapy mucositis feasibility study of manuka and kanuka essential oils in 19 patients, which reported delayed mucositis onset.[10][6][8][7] A systematic review compares essential oils with chlorhexidine.[2]

A 2007 recall covered about 4 million bottles of Listerine Agent Cool Blue over potential contaminants.[1] Wikipedia notes people sometimes drink mouthwash for intoxication and that links between alcohol-containing mouthwash and oral cancer are inconclusive.[1]

timeline.event: FTC rules cold and sore throat claims misleading.[1]
